lesson.title: How Biologists Ask Questions and Trust the Answers
lesson.summary: This section introduces the scientific method as a repeatable cycle of observation, questioning, and testing that lets biologists build reliable knowledge about living things.
lesson.body:
Biology is built on a simple but powerful habit of mind: do not just guess about how living things work, test your ideas against the natural world and be willing to change your mind when the evidence disagrees with you. The scientific method is the name for this habit, organized into a repeatable cycle. It usually starts with an observation, something a person notices about the world that raises a question. From that question, a scientist proposes an explanation, gathers evidence, and checks whether the evidence supports or undermines the explanation. The word "method" makes it sound like a rigid checklist, but in practice it is closer to a loop that scientists move through again and again, often skipping steps or circling back when new observations arrive.

A concrete historical example shows how the cycle works. In the mid 1800s, many scientists believed in spontaneous generation, the idea that living microorganisms could arise on their own from non-living broth, without needing to come from other microorganisms. Louis Pasteur observed that broth left open to air grew cloudy with microbes, while sealed broth stayed clear. This observation raised a question: did the microbes come from the air, or did they arise spontaneously inside the broth? Pasteur designed a now famous test using swan necked flasks, glass containers with long curved necks that let air reach the broth but trapped dust and microbes in the curve before they could reach the liquid. The broth in these flasks stayed sterile indefinitely, even though it was exposed to air. When Pasteur tilted a flask so broth touched the dust trapped in the neck, microbial growth appeared within days. This series of tests, not any single observation, is what convinced the scientific community that microorganisms come from other microorganisms rather than appearing out of nowhere.

Several features of this example generalize to all of biology. First, the explanation had to be testable: Pasteur could imagine an experiment that would come out differently depending on whether spontaneous generation was true. An idea that cannot be tested, even in principle, sits outside the reach of the scientific method. Second, the test had to be repeatable. Other scientists could build their own swan necked flasks and get the same result, which is part of why the conclusion became widely trusted rather than resting on Pasteur's word alone. Third, the process was cumulative. Pasteur's work built on earlier, less conclusive experiments by other researchers, and later scientists refined his techniques further as microscopy and sterile technique improved.

It is worth being clear about what the scientific method does and does not deliver. It rarely produces absolute proof. Instead it produces explanations that have survived repeated, serious attempts to disprove them, which is why biologists describe well supported explanations as strongly supported rather than proven beyond all possible doubt. This matters because later sections build directly on this cycle. Turning a general question into a testable statement is the subject of hypothesis testing, designing a fair test that isolates one cause is the subject of controlled experiments, and precisely defining what you change and what you measure is the subject of independent and dependent variables. Each of those skills is really just a more detailed look at one part of the same loop introduced here: observe, question, test, and revise.
